finding: The live range of $220-$775 looks about right for mainstream cars and trucks, but we could only partly verify it. Implied totals (parts + hours x $120-$160/hr): midsize 2016 Camry about $206-$865, where the labor span is only a bracket (0.8 hr is Toyota's warranty time for front pads alone on a Sienna; 3.5 hr is Toyota's time for machining rotors and replacing pads on a 2007-2010 Camry), so the top of that figure is overstated for a plain rotor swap; truck 2016 F-150 about $353-$630, using a parts seller's 1-hour install estimate rather than a book time. Economy (2015 Corolla) and luxury (2015 BMW 328i) totals could not be computed because no stated labor time was found for those vehicles; their parts alone run $100-$280 and $191-$228 (the BMW figure is aftermarket/OEM-brand only: genuine BMW rotors alone are about $230 a pair and no genuine pad price was found, so dealer parts cost is higher than shown). The live low end of $220 sits just under AAA's and KBB's $250 and near our lowest implied total of $206; the live high end of $775 is above AAA ($500) and KBB ($400) and covers our truck figure, but RepairPal's $574-$698 national average suggests many real quotes fall in the upper half of the range, and a dealer job on a European car with genuine parts can plausibly exceed $775. No change is supported by this evidence; the range is wide, but the spread between an aftermarket kit and list-price OEM parts is real.
extras: Quotes often add: brake hardware/clip kit and pad-wear sensors (European cars), brake fluid flush, caliper service or replacement if seized or leaking, rotor machining instead of replacement, shop supplies and disposal fees, inspection or diagnosis fee, and sales tax. The rear axle is priced separately.
